subject: computer-science
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which is a core responsibility of an operating system's memory management?
options: Allocating memory to processes and tracking which areas are in use
Encrypting all network traffic
Rendering 3D graphics
Setting the CPU clock frequency
questions.explain: Memory management allocates and frees memory for processes and keeps track of usage to prevent conflicts.

questions.q: What is the role of the control unit (CU) in the CPU?
options: It coordinates and directs the operation of the processor by decoding instructions and issuing control signals
It performs floating-point multiplication
It holds the data fetched from memory
It stores the next instruction's address
questions.explain: The control unit decodes instructions and sends control signals to coordinate the other components of the processor.

questions.q: Which register holds the address of the memory location currently being accessed?
options: Accumulator (ACC)
Memory data register (MDR)
Current instruction register (CIR)
Memory address register (MAR)
questions.explain: The MAR holds the address of the memory location to be read from or written to.

questions.q: In round-robin scheduling, each process is given:
options: Priority based on memory usage
Unlimited CPU time until completion
CPU time only when no other process is ready
A fixed time slice (quantum) before being preempted
questions.explain: Round robin allocates each process a fixed time quantum, cycling through ready processes fairly.

questions.q: A key characteristic of RISC processors is that they:
options: Have no general-purpose registers
Use a large, complex set of variable-length instructions
Cannot be pipelined
Use a reduced, simple set of instructions that typically execute in one cycle
questions.explain: RISC uses a small set of simple, fixed-length instructions designed to execute quickly, easing pipelining.

questions.q: After an instruction is fetched into the MDR, where is it transferred for decoding?
options: The program counter
The memory address register
The current instruction register (CIR)
The stack pointer
questions.explain: The fetched instruction is moved into the CIR (instruction register) where it is decoded.

questions.q: Why are CPU registers faster to access than cache or main memory?
options: They are accessed over the address bus
They use magnetic storage
They are larger in capacity
They are located inside the CPU and built from very fast circuitry
questions.explain: Registers are inside the CPU itself and use the fastest circuitry, giving near-instant access.

questions.q: How does an interpreter differ from a compiler?
options: An interpreter only works on assembly language
A compiler executes code without translating it
An interpreter produces a standalone executable file
An interpreter translates and executes the source line by line at run time
questions.explain: An interpreter translates and executes source code line by line, producing no separate object file.

questions.q: Paging divides memory into:
options: Variable-sized logical segments matching program structure
Single contiguous regions per process
Fixed-size blocks (pages/frames)
Sectors defined by the hard disk geometry
questions.explain: Paging splits memory into fixed-size pages (and frames), which need not be contiguous in physical memory.

questions.q: In the Little Man Computer (LMC) model, the accumulator is used to:
options: Store the entire program permanently
Store the address of the next instruction
Hold the result of arithmetic and the value being worked on
Manage input/output ports only
questions.explain: In LMC the accumulator holds values for arithmetic and the current working result.

questions.q: Which scheduling algorithm can lead to starvation of low-priority processes?
options: Priority scheduling
Round robin
First come first served
Shortest job first only when jobs are equal
questions.explain: Priority scheduling can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving.

questions.q: In the von Neumann architecture, program instructions and data are stored:
options: In the control unit's microcode store
In physically separate memories with separate buses
In the same memory, sharing a common bus
Only in CPU registers, never in main memory
questions.explain: The von Neumann architecture uses a single shared memory and bus for both instructions and data, unlike Harvard architecture.

questions.q: Compared with RISC, CISC architectures tend to:
options: Always run faster on every workload
Use complex, multi-cycle instructions and require less compiler effort
Have fewer addressing modes and simpler instructions
Lack a control unit
questions.explain: CISC provides complex instructions (often multi-cycle), shifting work from the compiler into hardware.

questions.q: Which translator converts assembly language into machine code, generally one-to-one?
options: Interpreter
Assembler
Linker
Compiler
questions.explain: An assembler translates assembly mnemonics into machine code, typically one assembly instruction per machine instruction.

questions.q: In a multicore processor, true parallel execution requires that:
options: Only one core is active at a time
The workload can be divided into tasks that run simultaneously on different cores
The clock speed is reduced for each core
All cores share a single register only
questions.explain: Multiple cores give true parallelism only when tasks can be split to run at the same time on separate cores.

questions.q: GPUs are particularly well suited to which type of task?
options: Tasks requiring very large individual registers and no parallelism
Highly parallel tasks performing the same operation on large data sets (e.g. graphics, ML)
Single-threaded operating system scheduling
Sequential tasks with many branches
questions.explain: GPUs contain many simple cores ideal for data-parallel work like rendering and matrix operations.

questions.q: When an interrupt with higher priority occurs, the processor typically:
options: Saves the current state, services the interrupt, then restores the state
Ignores it until the current program finishes
Resets the program counter to zero permanently
Deletes the current program from memory
questions.explain: The CPU saves its current state (registers/PC) onto the stack, runs the ISR, then restores the state to resume.

questions.q: How does segmentation differ from paging?
options: Segmentation cannot be used with virtual memory
Segments are variable-sized logical divisions; pages are fixed-size
Segments are fixed-size; pages are variable
Segmentation removes the need for an address bus
questions.explain: Segmentation divides memory into variable-sized logical units, whereas paging uses fixed-size blocks.

questions.q: Which feature distinguishes Harvard architecture from von Neumann architecture?
options: It only supports a single register
It has no arithmetic logic unit
It cannot execute stored programs
It uses separate memories and buses for instructions and data
questions.explain: Harvard architecture physically separates instruction and data memory, each with its own bus, allowing simultaneous access.

questions.q: Why does increasing clock speed not give a directly proportional increase in real-world performance?
options: Instructions become longer at higher speeds
Higher clock speeds reduce the number of cores
The PC stops incrementing at high speeds
Memory access, cache misses and heat/power limits create bottlenecks
questions.explain: Performance is limited by factors such as memory latency, cache misses and thermal/power constraints, not clock speed alone.

questions.q: Pipelining increases throughput by:
options: Removing the need for a control unit
Executing one instruction completely before fetching the next
Doubling the clock speed automatically
Overlapping the fetch, decode and execute stages of consecutive instructions
questions.explain: Pipelining overlaps stages of different instructions so several are in progress at once, increasing throughput.

questions.q: Which bus carries signals such as 'memory read', 'memory write' and clock pulses?
options: The address bus
The control bus
The expansion bus
The data bus
questions.explain: The control bus carries control signals that coordinate and synchronise the activities of the system.

questions.q: The width of the address bus directly determines:
options: The size of the cache only
The clock speed of the processor
The maximum amount of memory that can be addressed
The number of cores in the CPU
questions.explain: An n-bit address bus can address 2^n unique memory locations, so its width sets the maximum addressable memory.

questions.q: Which CPU component performs arithmetic and logical operations?
options: The memory address register
The arithmetic logic unit (ALU)
The program counter
The control unit
questions.explain: The ALU carries out all arithmetic and logical (Boolean) operations within the processor.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the stored-program concept?
options: Instructions are stored in memory and can be treated as data, fetched and executed sequentially
Programs can only run from ROM
Programs are hard-wired into the CPU permanently
Each program needs a separate physical processor
questions.explain: The stored-program concept holds that instructions are stored in memory alongside data and executed in sequence.

questions.q: During the fetch phase of the fetch-decode-execute cycle, the contents of the PC are first:
options: Sent to the ALU for processing
Compared with the accumulator
Copied into the MAR
Written back to main memory
questions.explain: The address in the PC is copied to the MAR so the correct instruction can be fetched from memory.

questions.q: Virtual memory allows a system to:
options: Eliminate the need for any RAM
Run programs larger than physical RAM by using secondary storage as an extension
Increase the actual clock speed of the CPU
Store data only in cache
questions.explain: Virtual memory uses disk space to extend apparent RAM, swapping pages in and out as needed.

questions.q: Cache memory improves performance primarily because it:
options: Permanently stores the operating system
Is faster than main memory and stores frequently used data/instructions close to the CPU
Has a larger capacity than main memory
Replaces the need for registers
questions.explain: Cache is small but very fast memory that holds frequently accessed data, reducing slow main-memory accesses.

questions.q: The program counter (PC) holds:
options: The instruction currently being decoded
The address of the next instruction to be fetched
The data most recently read from memory
The result of the last calculation
questions.explain: The program counter stores the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched in the cycle.

questions.q: A compiler offers which advantage over an interpreter for distributing finished software?
options: It produces machine code that runs without the source or translator present
The source code must be shipped with the program
Errors are always reported one at a time during execution
It executes more slowly than interpreted code
questions.explain: A compiler produces standalone executable machine code, so the source and translator need not be distributed.
